content: Anterior vaginal repair, also known as anterior colporrhaphy, is a surgical procedure traditionally employed to treat moderate to severe stress urinary incontinence (SUI) in women. SUI is a prevalent condition, affecting approximately one-third of adult women, and it imposes a significant health and economic burden on both the affected individuals and society. The objective of this analysis was to evaluate the effectiveness of anterior vaginal repair in managing urinary incontinence compared to other treatment options. A systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register (as of September 1, 2009) and reference lists of relevant studies. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials that involved anterior vaginal repair for urinary incontinence. Data extraction and trial quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, and additional information was sought from three trial investigators. A total of ten trials were identified, involving 385 women who underwent anterior vaginal repair and 627 women who received alternative interventions. Evidence from a single small trial was insufficient to compare anterior vaginal repair with physical therapy. When compared to bladder neck needle suspension, anterior vaginal repair demonstrated similar outcomes in terms of failure rates after one year (risk ratio [RR] 1.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.86 to 1.56). However, clinically significant differences could not be definitively excluded. No trials were available to compare anterior vaginal repair with suburethral sling procedures, laparoscopic colposuspensions, or other vaginal surgical techniques. Anterior vaginal repair was found to be less effective than open abdominal retropubic suspension, as evidenced by patient-reported cure rates. In the medium term (failure rates within one to five years), 38% of women experienced failure after anterior repair compared to 17% after retropubic suspension (RR 2.29, 95% CI 1.70 to 3.08). In the long term (failure rates beyond five years), 38% of women experienced failure after anterior repair compared to 21% after retropubic suspension (RR 2.02, 95% CI 1.36 to 3.01). Additionally, three trials indicated a higher likelihood of requiring repeat surgery for incontinence after anterior vaginal repair (23% vs. 2%; RR 8.87, 95% CI 3.28 to 23.94). These findings were consistent regardless of the presence of coexisting pelvic organ prolapse. Although anterior vaginal repair was associated with a lower risk of subsequent prolapse (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.47), the need for later prolapse surgery was similar between vaginal (3%) and abdominal (4%) procedures. Most of the data comparing anterior vaginal repair with open abdominal retropubic suspension pertained to Burch colposuspension. Limited data comparing anterior repair with the Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz procedure were consistent with findings for Burch colposuspension. In conclusion, there was insufficient evidence to compare anterior vaginal repair with physical therapy or needle suspension for primary SUI. Open abdominal retropubic suspension appeared to be superior to anterior vaginal repair based on subjective cure rates, even in women with concurrent prolapse. The need for repeat incontinence surgery was also lower following abdominal procedures. However, data on postoperative complications and morbidity were limited. A Brief Economic Commentary identified one study suggesting that vaginoplasty may be more cost-effective than tension-free vaginal tape (TVT-O).
